title: Thousands of years of indoor air pollution
gist: Yglesias traces how, despite humans controlling fire for at least 400,000 years, the chimney wasn't invented until 12th-century England and spread only slowly, meaning most of human history involved unventilated indoor open-hearth fires; the (paywall-truncated) article notes indoor smoke inhalation from open fires still kills millions of the global poor annually today.

themes.theme: The surprisingly late invention of the chimney

insights.claim: The chimney is believed to have been invented in England sometime in the 12th century and only slowly gained popularity over subsequent centuries, despite humans having used controlled fire for at least 400,000 years — meaning most of human history involved indoor fires without proper smoke ventilation.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: A striking historical baseline for how slowly a known, health-protective home technology diffused even after invention — a useful analogy for evaluating current slow-diffusion problems for known solutions (e.g., clean cookstoves) in emerging markets today.
insights.locator: 'The chimney, by contrast, seems to have been invented in England'

insights.claim: Archaeologists believe Ice Age humans roughly 20,000 years ago survived extreme cold by living in natural rock shelters enhanced with insulation, and spent summer nights in dome structures, with both types of shelter heated by open hearths in the middle of the space.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Establishes the multi-hundred-thousand-year gap between humans having fire technology and having any safe method of indoor combustion.
insights.locator: 'Archeologists believe Ice Age humans spent much of their time'

insights.claim: Early humans understood they needed some kind of opening in the ceiling for indoor fires or everyone inside would suffocate and die — a basic but critical safety adaptation that long predated the invention of the chimney.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: A minor historical data point on early fire-safety adaptation; low direct market relevance but useful background for the piece's broader indoor-air-quality argument.
insights.quote: People understood that you needed some kind of hole in the ceiling or everyone would suffocate and die.

insights.claim: Yglesias observes that pre-chimney open-hearth heating meant people were 'breathing absolutely filthy air all winter long' for thousands of years, a reality rarely depicted in historical fiction or fantasy (e.g., 'The Odyssey,' 'House of the Dragon') because, in his view, it would look too ugly and depressing on screen.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: A media-realism critique: historical/fantasy depictions of the past systematically understate the physical unpleasantness (indoor smoke, poor air quality) of pre-modern daily life.
insights.quote: something you rarely see depicted on screen because it would be ugly and depressing
insights.locator: 'But the upshot is still that people were breathing'

themes.theme: Indoor air pollution as an ongoing global health hazard

insights.claim: Indoor air pollution from open cooking and heating fires remains a major, ongoing public-health problem for the global poor today, with the article stating that millions of people die every year from respiratory and pulmonary problems caused by inhaling indoor smoke (the article is cut off by the paywall immediately after introducing this point).
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Reinforces the case for continued attention (NGO funding, impact investment, public-health policy) to clean cookstove and indoor-air-quality interventions as addressing a large, persistent global mortality burden; the article's fuller treatment of solutions is behind the paywall.
insights.quote: Literally millions of people die every year due to respiratory and pulmonary problems caused by inhaling smoke indoors.
